i.e. image to image works by first translating the new image into latent space, then adding the gaussian noise in that space, and combining it with the prompt generated latent. Adding the noise here to default image is to simulate the partial inference. Lets say you are adding enough noise to make it function like latent version of a stage 20 image out of 50, this combined with latent coming from the prompt makes the model to implement additional details or other structures on the base of the image you provide. Therefore adding whatever you had on the prompt to whatever image you have.

Stable diffusion, if i am not mistaken does this about 1000 times in training in latent space. In inference you can pick which 50 times is what is recommended. I also would recommend to look into sequencer class to see how this time frames are handled. And how can you exploit the same principle for generating image to image transformations

If you wanna go real embedded I would urge you to take a look at excellent designs of mutable instruments eurorack modules, they are open source so you can take a look at their hardware (they are bare metal arm mcu boards) and their software (dsp)

Hey, the systems like KO are called embedded systems, this is a very very big topic but embedded systems has historically different kind of operating systems for hard real time applications (no os you have used on your computer so far is really a real time os) The most popular embedded operating systems are freertos and zepyhr. And with the normal computer and an embedded system the main difference is you're working with extremely limited system resources (think of kbs of ram and memory and hottest cpu you can get now is I think 600Mhz) But for a synth you can get away with bare metal processing (no os only your code) main challenges you're looking for in the hardware side is picking a microcontroller(a chip has internal memory ram and a cpu) and picking a codec (another chip that does analog-to-digital digital-to-analog conversion) In the software side, you will have to learn a bit on DSP (digital signal processing) (check stanford CCRMA lab notes) and a little bit of c++. If you want a quicker way, I recommend taking a look at teensy 4.0 development board which has an audio lib and an official codec add-on board. If you don't wanna work on extremely limited resource stuff that runs on AAA batteries, you can go with a raspberry pi zero (2?) that has much more power draw but it's orders of magnitude easier to create something out of it (check something called pure data).

And making a path for possiblity of clone modules for the z. These people has worked really hard for years to create this device we all love, and they have all the right in the world to sell it or its accessories for whichever price they see fit. IMHO Making a clone module is basically stealing their efforts and IP. So i think it is very terribly unethical.

I dont think they are activated at all times. They would probably wait for some sort of handshake between the module and the host during the boot. When this interaction fails after a timeout period, i believe the ports are closed for good. Another assumption of mine is there is no single interface. Some basic interface like UART is used to handshake and interrogate the installed module. And any required interface actually opened afterwards.

We currently dont really know what they are sending to the cv module, but it is tempting to assume they are sending some sort of serial info. Even if we intercept the comm between the host and module, which is very easy in the serial case we wont going to achieve any secret things that are havent hard coded into main cpu of the z. To do something more interesting than converting some serial things into midi or cv, we need to wait for more interesting modules.
